author: Maria Montessori
quote: But mental development must be connected with movement and is dependent on it. This is the new idea that must enter educational theory and practice.
credit: Maria Montessori · The Absorbent Mind, 1949 (first edition, Adyar), ch. XIII, p. 203
meaning: Montessori told teachers that the growth of a child's mind is tied to movement and depends on it.

author: Roger W. Sperry
quote: In both its phylogenetic and ontogenetic histories, mental activity develops out of, and in reference to, overt action.
credit: Roger W. Sperry · "Neurology and the Mind-Brain Problem", American Scientist 40(2), April 1952, p. 299
meaning: A brain scientist who later won a Nobel Prize wrote that thinking grows out of doing, both in the long history of animals and in every growing child.

author: Aristotle
quote: Now it is clear that in education practice must be used before theory, and the body be trained before the mind
original: ἐπεὶ δὲ φανερὸν πρότερον τοῖς ἔθεσιν ἢ τῷ λόγῳ παιδευτέον εἶναι, καὶ περὶ τὸ σῶμα πρότερον ἢ τὴν διάνοιαν
credit: Aristotle · Politics VIII.3 (1338b4-6), about 330 BC · tr. Benjamin Jowett, revised by W. D. Ross (Oxford, 1921)
meaning: Aristotle said that in bringing up children, practice comes before theory and training the body comes before training the mind.

author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
quote: To learn to think we must therefore exercise our limbs, our senses, and our bodily organs, which are the tools of the intellect
original: Pour apprendre à penser, il faut donc exercer nos membres, nos sens, nos organes, qui sont les instruments de notre intelligence
credit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau · Emile, or On Education, 1762, Book II · tr. Barbara Foxley, 1911
meaning: Rousseau said our arms, legs and senses are the tools we think with, so we must use them to learn to think.

author: Gerd Kempermann and colleagues (Kempermann, Fabel, Ehninger, Babu, Leal-Galicia, Garthe, Wolf)
quote: In animals, most if not all aspects of cognition are inseparable from locomotion and physical activity.
credit: Gerd Kempermann and colleagues · "Why and how physical activity promotes experience-induced brain plasticity", Frontiers in Neuroscience 4:189, 2010
meaning: Scientists who study running mice wrote that in animals, almost all thinking and learning is tied to moving around.

author: John J. Ratey, MD (with Eric Hagerman)
quote: Building muscles and conditioning the heart and lungs are essentially side effects. I often tell my patients that the point of exercise is to build and condition the brain.
credit: John J. Ratey, MD, with Eric Hagerman · Spark: The Revolutionary New Science of Exercise and the Brain, 2008 (Introduction)
meaning: A doctor says he tells his patients that stronger muscles and a fitter heart are side effects, and that the point of exercise is to build up the brain.

author: Sir Charles Sherrington
quote: As we look along the scale of life, whether in time or in order of organization, muscle is there before nerve, and nerve is there before mind, 'recognizable mind'.
credit: Sir Charles Sherrington · Man on his Nature, 1940 (Gifford Lectures 1937-8), ch. VI, pp. 196-197
meaning: Looking at living things from simple to complex, a Nobel Prize scientist saw that muscle appeared first, then nerves, then mind.

author: Pyotr Lesgaft (П. Ф. Лесгафт)
quote: Mental growth and development require a corresponding physical development.
original: Умственный рост и развитие требуют соответствующего развития физического.
credit: Pyotr Lesgaft (П. Ф. Лесгафт) · Guide to the Physical Education of School-Age Children, Part I, ch. II (1888; text of the 2nd edition, 1904) · researcher's translation
meaning: A Russian doctor and teacher wrote that for the mind to grow, the body has to grow along with it.

author: Nikolai A. Bernstein (Николай Александрович Бернштейн; spelled "Nicholai A. Bernstein" on the 1996 English title page)
quote: Motor tasks (motor needs) and the implacable necessity to move more quickly, accurately, and dexterously were the leading causes for the development of the brain and its accessories during all the millenia of evolution.
original: Именно двигательные задачи, двигательные потребности, неумолимая жизненная необходимость двигаться все проворнее, все точнее, все ловче — вот что было ведущим началом в развитии мозга и всех его вспомогательных органов почти на всем протяжении его многовековой эволюции.
credit: Nikolai A. Bernstein · On Dexterity and Its Development (written late 1940s, first printed 1991) · tr. Mark L. Latash, 1996
meaning: A Russian scientist of movement wrote that the brain developed over a very long time mainly because animals had to move faster, more exactly and more skilfully.

author: John Dewey
quote: nature's "intention" ... is to develop the mind especially by exercise of the muscles of the body
credit: John Dewey · Democracy and Education, 1916, ch. 9, p. 135
meaning: Dewey said nature does not train the body first and the mind later: it grows the mind above all by using the muscles.

author: Swami Vivekananda
quote: You will understand the Gita better with your biceps, your muscles, a little stronger.
credit: Swami Vivekananda · "Vedanta in its Application to Indian Life", lecture in Madras, 1897 (Complete Works, vol. 3, p. 242)
meaning: A monk told young men they would understand their holy book, the Gita, better if their muscles were a little stronger.

author: Plato
quote: Let us assume, then, as a first principle in relation both to the body and soul of very young creatures, that nursing and moving about by day and night is good for them all
original: λάβωμεν τοίνυν τοῦτο οἷον στοιχεῖον ἐπʼ ἀμφότερα, σώματός τε καὶ ψυχῆς τῶν πάνυ νέων τὴν τιθήνησιν καὶ κίνησιν γιγνομένην ὅτι μάλιστα διὰ πάσης τε νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας, ὡς ἔστι σύμφορος ἅπασι μέν
credit: Plato · Laws, Book VII, 790c (about 350 BC) · tr. Benjamin Jowett, 1892
meaning: Plato wrote, as a first rule for raising the very young, that being nursed and kept moving day and night is good for both their body and their soul.

author: Galen
quote: When exercise can render service both to body and mind, each in its own special form of excellence, it is a blessing indeed.
original: οὐ σμικρὸν δὲ καὶ τοῦτ’ ἀγαθόν, ὅταν ἄμφω τὸ γυμνάσιον ὠφελεῖν δύνηται, καὶ σῶμα καὶ ψυχήν, εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν ἑκάτερον ἀρετήν.
credit: Galen · On Exercise with the Small Ball, ch. 3 (2nd century AD) · tr. F. A. Wright, Greek Athletics, 1925, p. 116
meaning: An old Greek doctor wrote that a ball game also sharpens the mind, and that exercise which helps both body and mind is a great good.

author: Socrates, as reported by Xenophon
quote: Why, even in the process of thinking, in which the use of the body seems to be reduced to a minimum, ... grave mistakes may often be traced to bad health.
original: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν ᾧ δοκεῖ ἐλαχίστη σώματος χρεία εἶναι, ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι, τίς οὐκ οἶδεν ὅτι καὶ ἐν τούτῳ πολλοὶ μεγάλα σφάλλονται διὰ τὸ μὴ ὑγιαίνειν τὸ σῶμα;
credit: Socrates, in Xenophon · Memorabilia III.12.6, about 370 BC · tr. E. C. Marchant (Loeb, 1923)
meaning: Socrates told a young man to train, because the body is used in everything we do, even in thinking, where bad health often causes big mistakes.

author: Charles H. Hillman and 9 co-authors (Pontifex, Castelli, Khan, Raine, Scudder, Drollette, Moore, Wu, Kamijo)
quote: The intervention enhanced cognitive performance and brain function during tasks requiring greater executive control.
credit: Hillman et al. · Pediatrics 134(4):e1063-e1071, 2014 (FITKids trial: 221 children, 9 months)
meaning: In this study, children who joined an active after-school program for nine months improved more than children on a waiting list at tests of ignoring distractions and switching between tasks.

author: Sushruta Samhita (attributed to Sushruta)
quote: A gentle walk or stroll, which is not very fatiguing to the body, tends ... to improve his memory, strength, digestive capacity (Agni) and the functions of the sense-organs.
credit: Sushruta Samhita · Chikitsasthana 24.80 · tr. Kaviraj Kunjalal Bhishagratna, vol. II, 1911, p. 491
meaning: An old Indian medical book says a gentle walk that does not tire the body much is good for memory, strength, digestion and the senses.

author: Svatmarama
quote: Salutation to Âdinâtha (Siva) who expounded the knowledge of Haṭha Yoga, which like a staircase leads the aspirant to the high pinnacled Râja Yoga.
original: श्रीआदिनाथाय नमोऽस्तु तस्मै येनोपदिष्टा हठयोगविद्या ॥ विभ्राजते प्रोन्नतराजयोगमारोढुमिच्छोरधिरोहिणीव ॥ १ ॥
credit: Svatmarama · Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.1, about 15th century · tr. Pancham Sinh, 1915
meaning: The old yoga manual says body-and-breath practice (hatha yoga) is like a staircase that leads up to the highest yoga of the mind (raja yoga).

author: Yan Yuan (顏元, 顏習齋)
quote: What is clear in the mind, spoken by the mouth and written on paper, if it has not been practised through the body, is all useless.
original: 心中醒，口中說，紙上作，不從身上習過，皆無用也。
credit: Yan Yuan (顏元, 1635-1704) · 存學編 (Cunxue bian), 卷二 〈性理評〉 · our translation
meaning: A Chinese teacher saw that he could talk about big ideas but got his times table wrong when he tried it, and said that knowing, saying and writing a thing is useless until you have practised it yourself, with your own body.
url: https://archive.org/details/02091872.cn (woodblock scan, image 51) ; https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/存學編/卷二

author: Tao Xingzhi (陶行知)
quote: Doing is the beginning of knowing; knowing is the completion of doing.
original: 行是知之始；知是行之成。
credit: Tao Xingzhi (陶行知) · 《行是知之始》 (Doing Is the Beginning of Knowing), talk of 3 June 1927 · researcher's translation
meaning: A Chinese teacher said doing comes first and knowing comes after, like a small child who learns that fire is hot by burning his hand.
url: https://archive.org/details/050260 (file "陶行知教育论文选辑 方与严编", leaf 39) ; https://archive.org/details/zslib_R-T (陶行知全集 第二卷)

author: Daniel Wolpert
quote: We have a brain for one reason and one reason only, and that's to produce adaptable and complex movements. There is no other reason to have a brain.
credit: Daniel Wolpert · TED talk "The real reason for brains", TEDGlobal 2011
meaning: A scientist who studies movement says we have a brain for one reason only: to make complex movements that can adapt.

author: Kirk I. Erickson, Michelle W. Voss, Ruchika S. Prakash and 15 others; senior author Arthur F. Kramer
quote: In sum, we found that the hippocampus remains plastic in late adulthood and that 1 y of aerobic exercise was sufficient for enhancing volume.
credit: Erickson, Voss, Prakash and 15 others (senior author Arthur F. Kramer) · PNAS 108(7):3017-3022, 2011
meaning: In this study, older adults who did a year of regular walking ended with a slightly bigger hippocampus (a brain area used for memory), while it got slightly smaller in the group that did stretching.

author: Karen E. Adolph and Justine E. Hoch
quote: Motor development is enabling: New motor skills create new opportunities for exploration and learning that instigate cascades of development across diverse psychological domains.
credit: Karen E. Adolph and Justine E. Hoch · "Motor Development: Embodied, Embedded, Enculturated, and Enabling", Annual Review of Psychology 70:141-164, 2019
meaning: Each new thing a baby learns to do with its body, like sitting, crawling or walking, opens up new things to explore and learn.

author: Konstantin Ushinsky (К. Д. Ушинский)
quote: ...we may with greater probability suppose that the history of the soul begins with the infant's first movements...
original: …мы с большей вероятностью можем предположить, что история души начинается с первых движений младенца…
credit: Konstantin Ushinsky (К. Д. Ушинский) · Man as the Subject of Education, vol. 1, ch. XIII, note to § 11 (1868) · researcher's translation
meaning: A Russian teacher supposed that a child's inner life begins with its very first movements.

author: Zhu Xi (朱熹)
quote: The ancients' elementary learning taught them through practical tasks, and that in itself nurtured their minds; without knowing or noticing it, they became good.
original: 古人小學教之以事，便自養得他心，不知不覺自好了。
credit: Zhu Xi (朱熹, 1130-1200) · 朱子語類 (Classified Conversations of Master Zhu), 卷七 · our translation
meaning: Zhu Xi said that in old times children were first taught things to do, like rites, music, archery and arithmetic, and that this practice shaped their minds before they were taught the reasons.
url: https://archive.org/details/06049691.cn (Siku Quanshu scan, 卷五~卷七) ; https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/朱子語類/007 ; https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/周禮/地官司徒
